comments.author: @kekui1647
comments.text:
4o is still better than o3 and o4 for actual programming. One-off prompts where you ask it to instantly write an entire game are edge cases — they don't really show which model is better. In fact, they skew the results. Newer models like o3 and o4 are tuned to "win" these quick tests, which forces them to chase being right on the first try, even if that means hallucinating way more than 4o would.

When you're actually coding — fixing bugs, adapting, thinking through problems — o3 and o4 often just make stuff up, while 4o stays grounded and can actually help you work through issues. It's like comparing a world-class athlete trained for one specific event versus someone who trained to be strong, fast, and durable overall. The specialist might dominate one narrow contest, but in every other real-world situation, the generalist outperforms them.

These newer models are being trained to beat metrics, not to be genuinely useful when it counts.

comments.author: @martini1179
comments.text: May I suggest a change to your methodology? Instead of giving these AI models a single prompt and a single chance to come up with a game, why don't you instead come up with a polished version of a single game with a lot of bells and whistles, and see if each model could create that game or not, and how close it would come to an ideal version of that simple game. This is to avoid any assumptions that any of these models make from the simple instructions about how the game should look and feel and play, and instead actually show what the model is capable of with multiple steps and iterations. I think that methodology would work better.
